title: We're in our 50s. Should we sell our house and buy a new landed home for semi-retirement?
excerpt: A couple in their early 50s want a double-storey home outside KL for semi-retirement and their parents, but fear new projects after one was abandoned. Sean backs the plan and says time your readiness, not the market.

question.asker: From Mrs I, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: Mrs I and her husband are in their early 50s, both work for multinationals and save about RM5,000 a month after expenses. They own a condo in Desa Petaling and a single-storey house in Kuala Lumpur, both paid off; their first property, 20 years ago, was abandoned for nine years before another developer finished it. In three years, once the children finish school, they plan to sell the single-storey house and buy a double-storey home of RM750,000 to RM880,000 in areas such as Semenyih, Salak Tinggi or Cyberjaya, also housing his parents.
question.text: Is this a sensible semi-retirement plan, are new projects safe, and should they buy new now or subsale later, given a friend says it's a bad time to buy?

answer.quote: Any time is the right time to buy.
answer.summary: Yes, if they can afford it: their 40s and 50s are when most people can finally choose a home for themselves rather than for work or school. Since they know the area, a subsale lets them see the exact house and negotiate; for new projects, today's laws make abandonment rarer. Don't wait for the right market, buy below the area's median price when you are ready.

reasons.title: A dream home fits this stage of life
reasons.body: Earlier, where you live is set by work and the children's schools. With the children nearly grown, they know what lifestyle they want and can afford, and selling a small single-storey house to fund a larger home elsewhere is a sensible trade.

reasons.title: Age shortens the loan
reasons.body: Banks lend until 65 or 70, so an RM800,000 house on a shorter loan may cost about RM3,000 a month. Make sure they are comfortable with that, plus renovation, before committing.

reasons.title: Abandoned projects are rarer, but costly
reasons.body: Since the Housing Development Act was strengthened, abandoned projects are less common. If it happens, buyers still repay the loan and interest on money the bank already released, so listed developers offer more certainty, at higher prices.

reasons.title: Timing the market is a guess
reasons.body: Ask whether the person saying it's a bad time owns property themselves. Every area has a median price; buying below it is good timing, buying far above it, as many did in Iskandar Malaysia, is the real risk.

actions: Stay in each shortlisted area a few times, for example in a homestay, before choosing.
Compare subsale houses in the same estates; you see the exact unit and can negotiate.
Check the area's median price per square foot and avoid paying well above it.
If a landed strata project limits changes to the façade, make sure that suits your renovation plans.
Decide whether this is purely a home or partly an investment, since that changes what you compare.
caveat: Whether the area suits them for daily life is something only they can judge. Sean also suggests they consider their hometown, which may give more value and keep them closer to family.
sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #215. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as the viewer and Sean stated them in July 2023. The captions garble the shortlisted project names, so they are left out.
